    💡 Key Takeaways
    • E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.
    • According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.
    • The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

    According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.

    The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.

    The Redmond-based firm recognized approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services during Q3.

    DocuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of the month's tracked spoofing activity. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also experienced increases toward the end of the quarter.

    The research found that some malicious messages were delivered despite failing e-mail authentication checks and being identified as threats.

    In September, tenant- or user-level security overrides applied to 63% of these messages with a recorded security outcome — most involved tenant-level exceptions.

    Microsoft warned that overly broad exceptions intended to support legitimate business communications can weaken protection against impersonation attacks.

    The organization emphasized that these findings do not establish whether recipients opened the messages or whether accounts were compromised.

    Microsoft also recorded approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3.

    Sources indicate that attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names instead of explicitly impersonating IT support personnel. Such display names accounted for 46% of an observed sample in July, rising to 88% in September.

    Meanwhile, QR code phishing declined 67% compared to Q2, totaling roughly 12.1 million attacks.

    Sources indicate that CAPTCHA-gated phishing activity increased toward the end of the quarter, reaching 3.1 million detected attacks in September. SVG attachments played a significant role in the increase.

    Credential theft remained the primary objective of malicious attachment campaigns, with approximately 94% to 96% of payload-based attacks directing owners to phishing sites or fraudulent sign-in pages.

    Microsoft recommended reviewing Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 configurations, enabling Safe Links and Safe Attachments, and strengthening authentication protections.

    The manufacturer also advised organizations to review security exceptions and verify the identities of external Teams contacts before responding to suspicious requests.

    For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.

    E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

    Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

    In a recent development, district and state policies run the gamut from embracing to banning AI. This raises a key question: When does AI accelerate student learning and when does it interfere?

    #66348. Tech Report: A Roundtable of Men in Their Nineties Taught Me the Secrets of Longevity

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2479 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: A Roundtable of Men in Their Nineties Taught Me the Secrets of Longevity

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2479 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor.
    • Alan Patricof, 92, is one of my idols.
    • Recent findings suggest that so when Patricof—who has also become one of my friends—called me with a request to join in on a lunch he was hosting for 12 men in their 90s, I was intrigued.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

    Alan Patricof, 92, is one of my idols. The legendary venture capitalist was an early investor in enterprises as varied as AOL, Apple, and New York magazine. More vital to me, aside from his incredible career and philanthropic work, he is a man who believes in always moving forward into the future. He co-introduced a fund called Primetime Partners when he was 85. At 88, he wrote his first book, No Red Lights: Reflections on Life, 50 Years in Venture Capital and Never Driving Alone. He was the oldest participant—and finisher—in the New York City Marathon at 88 and got remarried at 89 to the globally recognized art advisor Barbara Guggenheim.

    Recent findings suggest that so when Patricof—who has also become one of my friends—called me with a request to join in on a lunch he was hosting for 12 men in their 90s, I was intrigued. I have been reporting on longevity for several years now and lead a company called ROARforward focused on the subject. Patricof asked me to come and talk about what I had learned about longevity and the possibility of the 100-year life. I agreed, but I immediately thought of it differently—as a master class in wisdom and experience where I stood to learn at least as much from these men as they could learn from me.

    When I saw the list of guests, it was a bit intimidating. It included a former CEO of a Fortune 100 company, a vice chairman emeritus at one of the largest banks on the planet, a major real estate developer, and a man who has his name on one of the most prestigious health systems in Upcoming York. And those are just the ones who agreed to be identified—some asked to remain anonymous.

    Recent findings suggest that you get the idea: This was not an everyday group of 90-somethings but rather a gathering of highly accomplished, successful men who continue to thrive in a variety of industries and disciplines. That only made me more interested, though I imagined it might take some work to translate their habits and the ways they were spending their time into things more accessible to everyday people.

    Luckily, I would turn out to be wrong about that.

    As the men assembled in a private room at Patroon, a popular Manhattan restaurant, I saw that many of them already knew each other, some from as far back as grade school. As Patricof went over ground rules, including no talk of politics (both parties were represented) and no talk of sex (though Viagra did find its way into the conversation), they moved around the room, shaking hands, asking about wives and kids, and explaining what was keeping them busy.

    That was my first clue that the behaviors that helped these men stay robust into their tenth decade had little to do with wealth. Research has shown that cultivating deep, healthy relationships is one of the best things you can do to increase your chances of having a long, healthy life. These men were living examples of what that looks like, and it’s free. (Though not if you have your lunches at Patroon.).

    Industry observers note that these men took care of three major aspects of their lives: health, head, and heart. First, they were committed to a fitness regimen and healthy eating habits. Second, they were highly engaged and curious individuals who valued a strong sense of purpose. Third, each of them had deep relationships with loved ones, whether a spouse, family, or friends.

    Sources indicate that you may notice that these are all universal virtues. They’re also things that can give you a sense of fulfillment if you’re only in your 80s, or 70s, or even younger. They aren’t solely investments in the future. You do them now, and they benefit you now. Which is a good feeling and precisely what makes longevity worth it in the first place. As one of the men said, “If today is the last day of my life, I’ve had a helluva run.”.

    It has been revealed that “At 90, I tried boxing at a gym near my home in Harlem,” said George Hirsch, 92, before adding, proudly, that he went a full round. Hirsch was the longtime chairman of the Fresh York Roadrunners running club. While he is no longer out doing road races, he is on a treadmill four or five days a week in a walk-run regimen. He supplements that with rowing, the elliptical machine, weights, and, apparently, the occasional prizefight, in a 60-minute routine.

    It has been revealed that for a gathering men who were 90 or older, this was a remarkably healthy group. It’s true they all have had access to the best health care, but none had problems with challenges that come for everyone, like cognitive decline, diabetes, and heart disease. That word routine seemed to be the key. Routine, regimen—take your pick. These men make a point of committing to physical activity rather than just dabbling in it. One told me, “I think the secret to my life physically is that I’ve worked with the same trainer three days a week for 29 years,” adding that “even when I travel, I take my iPad and work out with him wherever I am.”.

    Industry observers note that in some cases, these routines would be the envy of any younger man! The men had all played some type of sports when they were younger and carried that behavior deep into their adult lives. Since movement and exercise are the top natural medicines for a long, healthy life, these guys were on it. Activities included walking, weight training, stationary bicycling, swimming, pickleball, tennis, and downhill skiing. Two of them have a regular tennis game, and one of the oldest in the group is still an avid golfer. Most of them go to a gym or have a personal trainer. While a few admitted that they were slower as they got older—a sign of remarkable maturity in a man, to admit that—they were all active.

    It has been revealed that they are also conscious of what they eat. They agreed that they consume less food than in the past and drink very little, if at all. As Hirsch said, “I never drank much, maybe a beer or glass of wine with a meal. But I don’t drink anymore—it just doesn’t mean that much to me.”.

    In a recent development, their attention to eating habits stood out. One thing that especially interested them was GLP-1’s, because of their impact on diet but also other potential benefits. As I shared what I’ve learned about longevity, including the frontiers of research on the topic, they asked question after question about the emergence of GLP-1’s and other classes of drugs that may enhance individual longevity. That kind of constant, engaged questioning was a hallmark of the group.

    Only one of the men at the lunch defined himself as “retired.” The others stated they were, at most, “semiretired.” While they are not necessarily working full throttle in what was their main career, to a man they all have very busy days—and that busyness, I found, is driven by a voracious curiosity, which is one of the best ways to strengthen and maintain brain health.

    Ken Langone is a great example. He came from a working-class family in Queens and is still in awe of his good fortune. He’s taken it to mean that, as long as he’s able, he should be doing everything he can not to squander what he has. “I won big, and I can’t tell you how grateful I am,” he said, adding, “We should be giving, not taking.”.

    He is in his office three days a week and works from home two days a week, engaged in a public board, three private boards, his family office, and other investments. His commitment to public health is incredibly important to him; he serves as chair emeritus of NYU Langone Health.

    “At 91,” Langone says, “my biggest issue is boredom, sitting around with nothing to do.”.

    Jim Freund, also 91, was a high-powered attorney into his early 60s, did a stint as a mediator after that, and now has a robust life as a writer, photographer, and musician.

    Recent findings suggest that he’s written 20 fiction and nonfiction books and has produced 25 albums of music featuring him at the piano. For six years, he has circulated a monthly blog for more than 500 friends and colleagues that includes the details of various projects he’s working on—an essay or short fiction, a piece of music, a portfolio of photos.

    According to recent reports, one expression of this curiosity is that all the men want to keep current. They follow the news, are dedicated readers, and have a deep curiosity about emerging trends. They don’t just read print; they’re on their phones, Kindles, Audible—anywhere there’s action. And AI—they’re on ChatGPT like everyone else. Some even have digital assistants.

    Recent findings suggest that but being current doesn’t just mean trendspotting. It can also mean having hobbies and projects that force you to engage with the world as it is. All of these men had ambitious upcoming endeavors in the works.

    Sources indicate that hirsch now has a bimonthly podcast with the running legend Amby Burfoot called “Running: State of the Sport.” Dan Rose, 97, former president and chairman of Rose Associates, the company that built Pentagon City and One Financial Center in Boston, is writing a latest book. Patricof and his wife are taking Yiddish lessons. At least one man reported that he was finally learning the piano.

    For all of them, it is crucial that their activities, whatever they may be, connect to deeper meaning and purpose.

    Industry observers note that larry Leeds, 97, the former CEO and chairman of the apparel tech giant Manhattan Industries, now works at Buckingham Capital Management five days a week buying and selling securities. It allows him to keep up with trends and investments. But it’s far from the most crucial thing to which he’s dedicated his energy.

    Leeds hopes the leading line in his obituary is the $27 million he raised to launch the Cary Leeds Center for Tennis and Learning in the South Bronx in 2015. Dedicated to athletic instruction and academic enrichment for underprivileged youth—health and head—the center is also an expression of the most important thing in Leeds’s life: his family. It is named after his son, who competed in six US Opens and five Wimbledon championships before dying at the age of 45.

    Sitting there in Patroon, I heard stories of how these men had committed to keeping themselves healthy and how their curiosity led them to continue to engage with the world at a point in their lives when they could just as easily have settled into insular routine. But it was the lunch itself that testified to their commitment to their hearts. Ninety years in, they were still making a point of getting together, speaking, laughing, and growing closer to other people.

    Upon arriving, as we sat and introduced ourselves, Patricof explained that he wanted to do this lunch not only to learn from one another at this stage of life but also to simply enjoy socializing with peers—like many women do on a regular basis. Women live five to six more years than men; maybe it is their commitment to deep relationships, he suggested, that is one of the key factors of their greater longevity.

    Women came up in another way too: Everyone attributed their health and longevity to having a loving partner.

    The majority of the men have had incredibly long marriages. Nine of the 12 had been married for more than 60 years. Two had been married for 70 years. Then there was Freund, who joked that he, too, has been married for 60 years—just not all to the same woman. (He is married to his second wife, and they are at 41 years and counting.).

    They all also have children and grandchildren, whom they are in touch with more than a few times a week—something any of us who are parents can do.

    Rose has a unique ritual. “We have a family video conference every Sunday night with family from all parts of the country. It’s life enhancing and a time to connect and give everyone a chance to share accomplishments and disappointments with each other,” he explained.

    It has been revealed that at this stage of their lives, many have lost longtime friends, but they all strive to make latest friends, some young, some old. In fact, there’s already a initiative in place to replicate the lunch so that a bunch of other 90-somethings can be invited into the conversation. Here’s the thing I noticed about this: What got these guys excited about another lunch wasn’t simply that they enjoyed each other’s manufacturer or having a laugh with peers about Viagra. They were also inspired by one other. That must count for something.

    Recent findings suggest that I walked away inspired, too, and in awe of how these men live. They have to walk a line that most of us don’t yet, and maybe never will. Part of being alive—especially for this group—is thinking about the future, trying to figure out what’s next, planning another pursuit, but now they all admit that their horizon of looking out, say, 25 years is no longer a reality.

    According to recent reports, in the face of that tension, they’ve found a way to be optimistic about their future while at the same time savoring the present. None complained about getting older. None talked about their aches and pains. Yes, they faced growing limitations, but they all seemed to take them in stride.

    “I do my best to love my life and try to have the same intensity and diligence that I had in my younger years,” noted Leeds.

    Langone mentioned, “When I can no longer take care of myself and I’m totally dependent on someone else, then that’s the time to go,” adding that “God has his plan.”.

    In a recent development, and Patricof has his. He’s already publicly stated that he intends to live to 114, which would be 22 more years. I pointed out that the world’s oldest verified living person, Ethel Caterham in the UK, just turned 117, and I challenged Alan to break that record. He gladly told me that he accepts the challenge, and I don’t doubt he’ll make a real run at it. I have to admit I have an ulterior motive: I look forward to my lunch with centenarians. And supercentenarians.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: The One Kitchen Feature Designers Always Splurge on—and Why It’s Worth It

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor.
    • Pictured above: Meghan Jay selected a brass chandelier with ribbed glass orbs to modernize this traditional kitchen.
    • The kitchen is the hardest-working room in your house, but it’s also one of the most expensive spaces to renovate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

    Pictured above: Meghan Jay selected a brass chandelier with ribbed glass orbs to modernize this traditional kitchen.

    The kitchen is the hardest-working room in your house, but it’s also one of the most expensive spaces to renovate. Depending on the size and scope of your redo, reimagining this space can cost up to six figures, so it’s notable to be wise about allocating your budget. While some people may overspend on high-end appliances or really luxurious countertops, you should never overlook the room’s lighting. Turns out, that’s where designers always splurge in the kitchen.

    It has been revealed that “Lighting has such a powerful ability to change how a room feels,” explains Meghan Jay, an interior designer in Winnetka, Illinois. “You can have the most beautiful cabinetry, stone, and hardware, but if the lighting isn't right, the space can feel flat or even cold.”.

    Meghan Meehan of Hudson East Design in New Jersey agrees and says the right fixtures can provide height, dimensionality, and lots of mood to the space. “Don't think of lighting as the finishing touch,” she adds. “Think of it as one of the main design elements that makes the entire kitchen.”.

    Ahead, here’s why spending a little more on your kitchen lighting is worth it—and exactly how much you should budget for.

    Recent findings suggest that every kitchen deserves to glow at full wattage, but it will cost you. After all, illuminating a kitchen isn’t as simple as adding a budget-friendly portable lamp and calling it a day: The best and brightest kitchens usually include several sources such as sconces, recessed ceiling fixtures, and under-cabinet lighting to illuminate meal-prepping zones.

    Sources indicate that “It needs to provide the right illumination for cooking and everyday tasks, but it also creates warmth and ambiance when you're entertaining or gathering with family,” Meehan explains. As a rule of thumb, she recommends homeowners allocate at least 8 to 12 percent of their kitchen renovation budget to lighting.

    Industry observers note that that said, anyone who wants to wow with some statement fixtures might wind up spending more. Jay, for example, suggests setting aside $3,000 to $7,000 for decorative wares such as pendant lights above an island.

    Admittedly, spending thousands of dollars on lighting is bound to elicit some sticker shock, and some people may wonder if it’s worth it. However, Lauren Wodicka insists it’s worth the investment. “Unlike a sofa, rug, or an appliance, lighting doesn’t experience the same daily wear and tear,” the Northern Virginia designer reasons. “A beautiful, well-made fixture can last for generations and become the focal point of a room.”.

    Sources indicate that oftentimes, less expensive fixtures can read cheap. “You may notice overly shiny or artificial-looking brass finishes, visible seams, thin metal, or cheaper-looking glass,” Jay says. “Higher-quality fixtures often have more substantial materials, beautiful patinas, and thoughtful details that become more apparent the closer you are.”.

    If you want to get the best bang for your buck, devise a shopping strategy. Santa Monica-based designer Christine Markatos Lowe first selects functional lighting and then spends the rest of her budget on “decorative pieces with personality.” But make no mistake, a personable light fixture should still have staying power: Lowe often reaches for timeless silhouettes from retailers like Urban Electric and Ann-Morris Lighting and is a sucker for details like handblown glass or “beautifully finished metals.”.

    It has been revealed that “The key to finding the right balance between statement lighting and a cohesive kitchen design is to make sure every element feels intentional,” Lowe explains. “It’s all about allowing each material or element to have its moment without overwhelming the space.”Wodicka—who calls Soane, Hudson Valley Lighting, and Visual Comfort her go-tos—notes less is more. “Not every kitchen island needs two or three lighting pendants,” she explains. “Sometimes one beautiful fixture can make a stronger statement.”.

    Designers often say lighting is the jewelry of a room, so layering different materials, sizes, and finishes adds more visual intrigue. Wodicka wants kitchen lights to complement each other—and the fixtures in surrounding rooms—but they don’t have to be identical. “A light fixture doesn't necessarily have to match the cabinet hardware or plumbing fixtures,” Jay adds. “I often prefer mixing finishes to create a more collected, layered look.”.

    In a recent development, if you want to keep your fixtures cohesive—without identical finishes—stick with a particular style. For example, a sconce with pleated fabric shades will look out of place next to a midcentury-style pendant that looks like it belongs on the set of Mad Men.

    For the perfect finishing touch, Meehan recommends putting all lights on dimmers, which is a simple detail that can make a huge difference. “This allows for functional lighting when cooking, but softer light to warm the space when you are entertaining,” she adds. And, if a small detail can make your investment work even harder, even better.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    The “Scottish Country House” Look Is the Cozy Interior Trend Designers Say to Know This Season

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor.
    • Sources indicate that you don't need a sprawling stone cottage in the Highlands, a sweeping countryside view, or a roaring fireplace to bring a little Scottish country-house charm into your home.
    • The secret is mixing those old-world details with pieces that feel fresh and livable, so your home doesn't end up looking like a period drama set.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

    Sources indicate that you don't need a sprawling stone cottage in the Highlands, a sweeping countryside view, or a roaring fireplace to bring a little Scottish country-house charm into your home. In fact, the appeal of this cozy, heritage-inspired aesthetic is that it can work just as beautifully in a city apartment as it does in a centuries-old estate.

    The secret is mixing those old-world details with pieces that feel fresh and livable, so your home doesn't end up looking like a period drama set. A tartan runner on the dining table, a cashmere throw draped over your favorite reading chair, or a few leather accents on the coffee table can bring just the right amount of countryside character to an otherwise modern space. Strathberry's fresh tartan homeware collection is another lovely entry point, giving the traditional pattern a contemporary spin that feels right at home in all kinds of interiors.

    Whether you're fully embracing your countryside daydreams or just looking to make your space feel a little warmer and more layered this winter, there are plenty of ways to bring the look home. Read on for the Scottish country-house-inspired touches that make this aesthetic so charming—and how to work them into your own space.

    Sources indicate that if there's one pattern that deserves a starring role in a Scottish country-inspired home, it's tartan. And you don't have to limit it to a throw blanket or a few accent pillows. Designer Kaitlin Smith recommends “using plaid for a wallpaper or even as an accent pillow” to bring that distinctly Scottish feel into a space.

    For a bolder take, try a tartan wallpaper in a powder room, entryway, or tucked-away reading nook. If you'd rather ease into the look, a single plaid pillow or upholstered accent piece can make just as much of a statement. With so many different tartan patterns and colorways to choose from, you can find one that brings a little heritage-inspired character to your home without making the whole room feel like a theme.

    In a recent development, A Scottish country house should feel like it's been lived in for generations, not styled within an inch of its life. That's where woven baskets come in.

    Noel Gatts, a designer and HGTV personality, recommends introducing “some slouchy woven baskets” throughout the home, whether at the entryway for shoes and umbrellas or in a living room or bedroom to hold extra blankets. Their slightly relaxed shape and natural texture add to that collected, lived-in feeling while giving everyday clutter somewhere to go.

    Try a larger basket beside the front door, a smaller one tucked under a console or an oversized version next to your favorite reading chair. It's a practical detail that also brings in the natural materials that make this aesthetic feel so grounded. Plus, having a cozy throw within arm's reach is never a bad idea.

    You can practically picture a pot of tea warming by the fire in a Scottish country house, and Gatts recommends leaning into that feeling with a thoughtful arrangement of crockery and candles.

    “Feature a fireplace or dining table with tea pots, earthenware, and an installation of candles and/or candlesticks,” she suggests. This is a lovely opportunity to bring out those pieces you might otherwise save for special occasions, from vintage teapots and handmade ceramic bowls to mismatched candlesticks and well-loved serving dishes. Grouping them together creates a charming focal point without making the space feel overly formal.

    Candlelight is especially important here, adding a soft, welcoming glow that feels worlds away from bright overhead lighting. And if you don't have a fireplace, a dining table, mantel or console can give you the same cozy effect.

    Sources indicate that A Scottish country house shouldn't feel too coordinated, so don't be afraid to bring a few different patterns into the mix. As designer Sarah Cole suggests, “try pairing a wool plaid with a botanical print, a small geometric pattern or a traditional rug.”.

    The combination adds visual interest and gives a room that layered, lived-in quality that makes country-house interiors so inviting. You can keep the look cohesive by pulling a few warm, autumnal colors throughout the patterns—like russets, burgundies, forest greens and ochres—while varying their scale so they don't compete with one another. It's a simple way to make the space feel more personal and collected over time.

    The Scottish country-house look has a wonderful appreciation for pieces that feel like they've been around awhile. Rather than filling every surface with brand-upcoming accessories, Gatts suggests bringing in “found objects with a sense of history” made from weathered wood, pottery, or patinated brass. These are the kinds of details that give a room its personality, whether it's an old wooden box on a coffee table, a vintage ceramic vessel or a brass object with a little wear and patina.

    Don't worry about everything matching, either. A mix of materials and finishes makes the space feel more authentic and less like you ordered the entire room in one shopping trip. Gatts recommends using these pieces on a coffee table for “the perfect antique flair,” but a bookshelf, sideboard, or entryway console would work just as well.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, a few well-chosen antique details can give a room that Highland lodge feeling without requiring a full redesign. Jill Wheeler of Birch Hill Interiors recommends adding “a touch of polished brass like antique candlesticks or wall sconces to give the space a refined look.” Try styling a pair of vintage brass candlesticks on a mantel, placing one on a coffee table, or swapping in brass wall sconces beside a favorite reading chair.

    Wheeler also suggests incorporating antiques on a mantel, coffee table, or built-in, noting that “antiques can help bring the outside in and tell a story.” The mix of aged finishes and meaningful finds adds a sense of history and character that makes a Scottish country-inspired space feel genuinely lived in.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor.
    • After years of quiet luxury, soft neutrals, and interiors that favor understated details, a little drama feels like a very welcome change.
    • In a recent development, the look also ties into Neo Deco, a modern take on Art Deco that brings together glamorous materials, bold silhouettes, and a fresh approach to decorating.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

    After years of quiet luxury, soft neutrals, and interiors that favor understated details, a little drama feels like a very welcome change. High-gloss furniture is making a comeback, bringing shine, color, and a bit of personality back into our homes. Whether it's a lacquered accent table, a sculptural console, or a statement cabinet with a reflective finish, these pieces have a way of catching your eye and making even the simplest room feel more interesting. And honestly, who indicates every piece of furniture has to blend into the background?

    In a recent development, the look also ties into Neo Deco, a modern take on Art Deco that brings together glamorous materials, bold silhouettes, and a fresh approach to decorating. But you don't need to turn your living room into a scene from The Great Gatsby to get in on it—a single glossy piece can add just the right amount of contrast to a neutral space, while mixing lacquer with natural wood, textured upholstery, or warm metallic accents keeps things feeling layered and livable.

    Ahead, designers share how to bring high-gloss furniture into your home and embrace a little more shine without going over the top.

    It has been revealed that not ready to go all-in on the high-gloss trend? An accent table is your low-commitment, high-impact way in. Tucked beside your favorite armchair or pulled up next to the sofa, a lacquered side table brings just enough shine to make the whole corner feel a little more interesting. The best part is the contrast, so have fun mixing finishes. Carol Alda, interior designer at Z Gallerie, loves pairing a glossy table with a “velvet or textured woven chair.” Just make sure the table sits at a comfortable height next to the chair so you can actually use it for your coffee (or cocktail).

    Color is another way to make the piece feel right at home. Ali Esmaili, design expert and owner of Esmaili Rugs, suggests pulling the shade of your accent table from a patterned rug, which creates an easy connection between the two. An oxblood, emerald, or classic black table brings plenty of Neo Deco attitude, especially in a sculptural shape. It's a small swap, but one that can give even the most neutral living room a welcome dose of personality.

    A little high-gloss feels right at home in a bar or entertaining area, where a touch of drama is practically part of the assignment. A lacquered bar credenza or sideboard in a saturated shade can turn your glassware and favorite bottles into a whole display moment.

    Jennifer Fitzpatrick, founder of Studio J & Co., explains that high-gloss finishes bring extra energy to a room by reflecting daylight and catching the flicker of candles and lamps in the evening. In a bar area, that means your decanters, glassware, and cocktail accessories get their own little spotlight. Fitzpatrick recommends pairing high-gloss pieces with unlacquered brass, fluted glass, and textured textiles.

    The coffee table is already the unofficial centerpiece of the living room, so why not give it a little extra attention? A lacquered version in a rich color or an unexpected shape can instantly make the space feel more interesting. And don't worry about all that shine feeling too formal. Fitzpatrick says today's high-gloss pieces are all about sculptural shapes, from curved profiles to clean geometric forms. A lacquered cocktail table can also catch the glow of your lamps in the evening, adding a little atmosphere without visually crowding your seating arrangement.

    Sources indicate that to keep the look feeling relaxed, mix that reflective surface with pieces that have plenty of texture. Esmaili loves pairing high-gloss furniture with vintage rugs, noting that “the gloss adds depth, movement and a touch of theatre.” The contrast between a shiny coffee table and a well-loved rug with plenty of pattern and texture gives the room a more layered, lived-in feel. Add a soft sectional and a few simple accessories, and you've got a statement piece that still feels right at home.

    “I prefer my jeans to hug up top, drape down low. This year, the brand’s entire site (minus a few exclusions) will be 40 percent off from November 23 to December 1, with early access starting November 19 for Red Tab Members. While you can find Levi’s markdowns at Amazon and other major retailers, you’ll find the widest range of washes, inseam lengths, and specialized fits by going straight to the source.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Fans are already counting down the days until we see Allie and Dean’s love story pan out on Off Campus season 2, and I don’t blame them one bit. It’ll be a minute until we reunite with the Briar U gang, but fans are keeping up with every revision on the TV adaptation of Elle Kennedy’s book series in the meantime. And the latest news on season 2 is that a certain cast member won’t be returning.

    “I’m not gonna be in the next season,” Riley Davis, who plays Allie’s ex-boyfriend Sean on the Prime Video series, told People at the New York City premiere of his movie November 1963 on November 18.

    Industry observers note that as for the reason behind his exit? Riley indicates there were some scheduling conflicts—which checks out, since he has a role in another YA series, Netflix’s Crew Girl. It’s unclear whether that particular project played a part in his departure from Off Campus.

    In a recent development, “There was a strategy for some Sean in season 2, and we just had a bit of a scheduling thing on my side and a bit on their side,” he explained. “So we’ll see what happens down the line.”.

    What’s more: Riley’s exit could potentially signal that the second season of Off Campus might go a different direction from the book series it’s based on.

    As viewers saw in the show’s first season, Riley’s character, Sean, plays a pivotal role in Allie and Dean’s romance. In the books, he and Allie have an on-again, off-again relationship—but we might not see that pan out now that Riley is out.

    This isn’t the first time the TV adaptation shook things up with some changes from the source material. In season 1, the show’s writers introduced John Logan’s nonbinary sibling Jules Logan, who noticeably wasn’t in the OG book series.

    We’ll have to see how Riley/Sean’s absence is really handled when Off Campus season 2 hits Prime Video on April 28, 2027!

    #66327. Inside a Denver Tudor That Blends English Eccentricity With Family-Friendly Design

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1244 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housebeautiful ↗ Open Full Page

    Inside a Denver Tudor That Blends English Eccentricity With Family-Friendly Design

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, when designer Kaitlyn Hoffman and her family returned to the United States after eight years in London, they had grown accustomed to the tighter quarters that city living often dictates.
    • “The biggest design challenge was anticipating how we would actually live in the home,” Hoffman indicates.
    • The nine-month project, which also introduced her firm, Studio Proper Design, restored the home’s Tudor character.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, when designer Kaitlyn Hoffman and her family returned to the United States after eight years in London, they had grown accustomed to the tighter quarters that city living often dictates. Needless to say, settling into a five-bedroom Tudor in Denver’s Cheesman Park neighborhood was a major leap. Built in 1900, the house was in good condition when Hoffman and her husband bought it, but earlier renovations had left it feeling at odds with its architectural style.

    “The biggest design challenge was anticipating how we would actually live in the home,” Hoffman indicates. Because they renovated the space before moving in, she had to guess at everything from where they’d gather to how the house would work for their two young kids. “Ultimately, it was an exercise in designing for a life we hadn’t quite experienced yet and trusting our instincts about how we wanted to live.”.

    The nine-month project, which also introduced her firm, Studio Proper Design, restored the home’s Tudor character. Hoffman and her partners at Alter Design + Build gutted the primary and powder bathrooms, overhauled the kitchen, and made smaller updates almost everywhere else. Along the way, plenty of the home’s charming original details got a second life: A pair of French doors found in the basement now anchors a custom pantry, and diamond-pattern mullions in the primary bath windows make the room look as though it had always been part of the house.

    The result is a home that reflects Hoffman’s signature “Brit-ish” style: layered, collected, and not too precious. “I think the magic is in the mix,” she indicates, crediting her years abroad with inspiring a fondness for eccentricity, coziness, and humor in her design projects. Even the house’s lore fits the mood. Neighbors insist it’s the former home of ‘60s country-rock group Nitty Gritty Dirt Band—though Hoffman admits she’s never been able to confirm it. “Whether it’s true or not, it’s fun to imagine that these walls might have witnessed a little rock-and-roll history.”.

    FAST FACTSDesigner: Kaitlyn Hoffman of Studio Proper DesignDesign Partner: Alter Design + BuildStylist: Natalie WaradyLocation: Denver, ColoradoThe Space: A five-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bathroom Tudor across 6,345 square feet.

    According to recent reports, A place where the whole family gathers and hosts, this living room is packed with personality and beloved furnishings, many of which have changed hands in the family throughout the years. While the decor is decidedly eclectic, the architecture itself is classic and stately. “We wanted this room to have the elegance of a traditional English drawing room, so we introduced egg-and-dart crown molding and a hand-carved Louis XV–style marble fireplace to give the space a greater sense of formality and architectural presence,” Hoffman shares.

    According to Hoffman, this area saw a true “everything but the kitchen cabinets” renovation. Existing wall ovens gave way to a freestanding range with a custom hood, and a new pantry took their place. It’s built around a pair of original French doors she found in the basement, adding key storage while hiding away the appliances.

    According to recent reports, to soften the modern lines, she added a paneled backsplash, unlacquered brass hardware, and sealed walnut butcher block countertops for a warm, rustic touch. “I wanted a kitchen that worked hard for our family but felt every bit as inviting as the rest of the house,” Hoffman adds.

    Though the dining room shares space with the living room, both areas needed to have distinct identities. To make guests feel like they’re entering into a completely separate room, Hoffman sourced several statement-making pieces. “I found all six antique Louis-style dining chairs on Facebook Marketplace for just $100, while the mirrored faux-bamboo armoire is a favorite piece we brought back with us from London,” Hoffman indicates.

    Recent findings suggest that tucked beneath the stairs between the kitchen and living room is a clever nook for mixing up the drink of the hour. “This multipurpose space houses my husband’s (many!) coffee supplies by day and transforms into a bar by night,” Hoffman states. Like in the kitchen, she preserved the existing cabinetry and gave it a fresh coat of blue paint, upcoming Negresco honed granite countertops, wallpaper, and updated fixtures. Now, it rivals the kitchen as the go-to entertaining spot in the home.

    According to recent reports, while gut-renovating this powder room, Hoffman fell in love with the botanical wallpaper, and she would’ve covered the entire space in it if it were a little more kid-friendly. “I opted for wainscoting on the lower half of the walls to protect the wallpaper from sticky fingers,” she states.

    This is one of two generously sized guest bedroom suites, so friends and family will never feel short-changed when it’s time to hit the hay. It also has some of the most intriguing decorative details in the entire house. “The gingham four-poster bed is the star of the room, and I love the playful contrast between its bold check and the floral Roman shades,” she states. The wall accents are equally as enviable. “The framed Hermès scarf is another longtime favorite, which I sourced at Round Top over a decade ago, before Round Top was cool!”.

    It has been revealed that hoffman took a light-touch approach to her daughter’s room, knowing that the seven-year-old would eventually want to put her own stylistic signature on it. “I wanted to create a room that felt charming and playful without being overly childish, with pieces she could continue to enjoy as she grows,” she notes. Beyond painting the walls a pretty blush pink, the only real change here was adding custom Roman shades, which give the room a more tailored, finished feel.

    This primary bathroom saw a full gut renovation to bring it up to the standards of modern living. Along with adding his-and-hers sinks and a freestanding tub, Hoffman took the opportunity to correct an architectural eyesore: the two mismatched windows that created irritating asymmetry. “We ultimately replaced both windows, incorporating diamond-pattern mullions in the upper third to complement the home’s Tudor architecture,” she adds. “It was a significant expense, but it gave us greater flexibility with the layout and brought a sense of continuity to the room.”.

    This guest room is an homage to the family’s life in London, as much of the decor came from their former home across the pond. The art, too, was sourced from a local printmaker whose studio was down the street in the family’s old neighborhood. Any new additions here were smaller and strategic. “The Schumacher floral fabric on the curtains and pillows became the thread that tied everything together, bringing color, pattern, and a sense of cohesion to the room,” Hoffman notes.

    The kids’ bathroom was reworked with total flexibility in mind. “With a son and a daughter sharing the space, I wanted a palette that felt playful and fresh without leaning either too feminine or masculine,” Hoffman notes. While the existing floor tile stayed, she added a custom double vanity so both kids can brush their teeth at the same time, as well as painted beadboard wainscoting to extend the country-home atmosphere into the washroom.

    Recent findings suggest that kaitlyn Hoffman is the founder of Studio Proper, a boutique residential interior design firm located in Denver, Colorado. She’s a British citizen and lifelong Anglophile whose signature style was honed over nearly a decade living in London. Her design sensibility takes inspiration from traditional English interiors but adds a modern, practical twist.

    #66324. Movado’s New Tempo-Matic Watch Is Inspired by an Iconic Piece from the ’70s

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (276 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

    Movado’s New Tempo-Matic Watch Is Inspired by an Iconic Piece from the ’70s

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (276 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Movado was founded in 1881 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, which isn’t a particularly odd backstory for a heritage Swiss watch brand.
    • Right now, a growing band of horological nerds is finding rich pickings in the Movado back catalog and pushing up vintage prices considerably—especially for its mid-century chronographs and its legendary Museum Watch (which celebrates 80 years in 2027; more of that to come) in the process.
    • According to recent reports, it’s not only the collectors who are digging into Movado’s past, however.

    Movado was founded in 1881 in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, which isn’t a particularly odd backstory for a heritage Swiss watch brand. But it has been American owned since 1983 and has a distinct quality tied deeply to its long history in the U.S. market—which puts it slightly outside the predictable purview of many watch collectors.

    Right now, a growing band of horological nerds is finding rich pickings in the Movado back catalog and pushing up vintage prices considerably—especially for its mid-century chronographs and its legendary Museum Watch (which celebrates 80 years in 2027; more of that to come) in the process.

    According to recent reports, it’s not only the collectors who are digging into Movado’s past, however. Last month, the brand released the Heritage Tempo-Matic ($995–$1,095), a re-creation of a watch that merges sporty and retro design in a neat and slinky package. The Tempo-Matic, Movado’s first automatic movement, was introduced in 1945 and went on to power a broad range of Movado’s wristwatches. But the rounded yet boxy “TV” shape of the upcoming Heritage Tempo-Matic is unmistakably 1970s, when watch design took a giant leap forward into sexy new territory.

    The 2026 version is available in three executions, each powered by the reliable Sellita SW200-1B movement and fitted with integrated steel bracelets that positively scream seventies. Two of them come in brushed steel with vertically brushed burgundy or blue dials. A third—which, we must admit, is our favorite—is gold-tone PVD with a warm gray dial. You’d be hard-pressed to find such an elegant, authentic, and affordable homage to the 1970s—a decade that’s presently a very hot motif in watch-collecting circles—anywhere else.

    #66308. Breaking: ELLE Decor Checks In: The Cooper, Charleston

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (595 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Elledecor ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: ELLE Decor Checks In: The Cooper, Charleston

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elledecor

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Founded as a seaport more than 350 years ago, Charleston evolved into one of the most crucial trade hubs in colonial America.
    • In a recent development, located on the site of the former State Ports Authority headquarters (which was demolished in 2019), the 191-key property sits on Charleston’s historic peninsula and overlooks the Cooper River.
    • “We wanted The Cooper to feel like a natural extension of the city, balancing the ease of a waterfront home with the refinement of a luxury hotel,” says Jun Chun, principal at Champalimaud Design.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Founded as a seaport more than 350 years ago, Charleston evolved into one of the most crucial trade hubs in colonial America. As the South Carolina city’s wealth grew, handsome estates began filling up its coastline. But throughout Charleston’s rich, colorful, and complicated history, the city never had a high-end hotel that took full advantage of its waterfront setting—until this year, with the debut of The Cooper.

    In a recent development, located on the site of the former State Ports Authority headquarters (which was demolished in 2019), the 191-key property sits on Charleston’s historic peninsula and overlooks the Cooper River. Interiors by Champalimaud Design pay homage to the city’s maritime heritage, referencing the “Lowcountry” culture that took root in the surrounding region.

    “We wanted The Cooper to feel like a natural extension of the city, balancing the ease of a waterfront home with the refinement of a luxury hotel,” says Jun Chun, principal at Champalimaud Design. “The overall inspiration was Charleston itself, particularly its coastal heritage, architectural history, and gracious, unhurried way of life.”.

    The six-story property, which is operated by Beemok Hospitality Collection, has a relaxed feel infused with a subtle Southern flavor. The experience starts before guests even step inside thanks to an entryway lined with an allée of crepe myrtle trees—a Charleston staple with tumbles of showy, hot-pink blooms.

    Recent findings suggest that inside, the lobby sports creamy marble flooring with a basketweave pattern that nods to the local art of braiding sweetgrass. Meanwhile, a mural inspired by changing tides lines the spiral staircase, leading to the public areas upstairs.

    The hotel’s Mediterranean-style signature restaurant, The Crossing, helmed by chef Nick Dugan, was designed by multidisciplinary studio Meyer Davis. (There are three additional, smaller dining venues on site.) For the restaurant’s meandering floor strategy, the design team created a series of distinct indoor and outdoor spaces, hewing to a marshland palette of soothing neutrals and calming blues as well as strategic doses of lacquer, teak, and honey onyx.

    It has been revealed that references to the local culture continue in the guest rooms, which feature bespoke headboards, wardrobes, and credenzas adorned with woven details, once again tying back to vernacular craft. “We approached the guest rooms as elegant waterfront homes rather than traditional hotel rooms,” states Chun. “Wide-plank oak floors, painted shiplap walls, woven textures, and residential-style Roman shades establish a sense of warmth and familiarity.”.

    According to recent reports, among the amenities are a 7,000-square-foot spa as well as a heated saltwater infinity-edge pool on the fourth-floor terrace. The pool deck, which has its own bar, overlooks not just the harbor but even more perks: a new waterfront park by Rees Roberts + Partners plus a private marina, where guests can charter one of the property’s cruising vessels, such as a Hinckley motor yacht.

    For the design team, bringing The Cooper to life was a careful balance of respecting tradition while also looking forward. “Charleston has an extraordinary architectural heritage and a strong tradition of craftsmanship, and we wanted to acknowledge those qualities without simply reproducing the past,” explains Chun.

    “Ultimately, we wanted The Cooper to feel as though it belongs in Charleston today and will continue to feel relevant for years to come.”.

    According to recent reports, geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

Sure, you can often score pieces from Lululemon’s “We Made Too Much” section, but that’s mostly limited to “get it before it’s gone” colors and styles.

    Starting November 19, through Cyber Monday on November 30, Lululemon is offering up to half off editor-approved styles, whether you’re shopping for holiday gifts, want to replace your worn-out joggers, or are already looking ahead to your “Work out more” Fresh Year’s resolution and need to patch your gym wardrobe accordingly.

    Shop Lululemon’s Black Friday sale.

    At some point, Lululemon morphed from solely being the retailer we’d turn to for workout wear to a place where you could feasibly handle most of your wardrobe needs, courtesy of the brand’s fan-favorite ABC pants, comfortable button-downs, and solid range of outerwear, all of which are included in the brand’s Black Friday markdowns.

    Industry observers note that we’ve gone so far as to dub these pants “iconic,” thanks to their versatility. They’re almost like denim in that way—easy to wear with casual pieces but also able to be dressed up in a pinch. Per Jonathan Evans, style director, the ABCs are a “smart, performance-minded essential that you can comfortably pull on every day.” Need we say more?

    Of course, Lululemon’s true bread and butter will always be athleisure. Right now, editor-endorsed joggers, T-shirts, and shorts—for those who are partial to showing a little leg year-round—are available for a fraction of the price.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As you whip up a weeknight meal or prep for a dinner party, you might find yourself daydreaming—and envisioning the kitchen you wish you had. While your current cook space might be perfectly functional, it just doesn’t have the aesthetics you long for.

    Alas, the kitchen is widely regarded as the most expensive room to renovate. As Houzz reports, the average cost to remodel a kitchen is at the moment $26,500. But if you’re happy with things like cabinets and appliances (or a renovation is far off in the future), and you want to focus on just the visuals, you can give the space a glow-up with as little as $100.

    It can indeed be done, and ahead, designers are sharing their best budget-friendly upgrades.

    Industry observers note that rugs are such thrift-able items. A good rug is basically a necessity in a kitchen, and it can easily be swapped with a new one that refreshes the visuals.

    Brooke Mennen-Talsma, principal interior designer at Brooke MT Interiors, shares that in the above kitchen she designed, she added a thrifted runner that she discovered for just $40, adding a focal point to an arched pantry.

    She says to not underestimate the power of secondhand, and a lot of her favorite pieces in her portfolio are thrifted items.

    It has been revealed that switching in fresh hardware for your cabinets is something that can be done in an afternoon, and it can be gentle on the wallet, too. You can also choose to add backplates to your existing hardware, as Sherrell Neal of Sherrell Design Studio recommends. She calls it a “quick upgrade that can stay under $100,” depending on the size and number of cabinets.

    While new lighting in a kitchen can quickly add up, you can add light in other, more economical ways.

    In a recent development, for instance, as Kira Young, founder and principal designer at High Tide Design, says, you can simply go with a “cute countertop lamp with a pretty little shade.” She advises specifically purchasing a rechargeable lamp, with no messy cords and no need for an outlet. It can also be easily moved anywhere.

    Sources indicate that homeowners are increasingly opting for collected, and even pleasantly cluttered, looks in their homes. But if you really want your kitchen visuals to look polished and pleasing, Heather Kirk, principal interior designer at Kirk Riley Design, suggests highlighting a “hero piece,” or a favorite item that shines and steals focus.

    Think strong statement pieces that offer both beauty and function, “like a cheerful tea kettle on the stove or a dramatic footed bowl on the counter,” as Kirk recommends.

    Emily Spanos, creative director of Emily June Designs, says that in one kitchen she designed, she painted only the lower cabinets a bright turquoise and kept the walls and upper cabinets a soft white. Paint is one of the cheapest ways to quickly upgrade a home, and it’s something that can effectively be used in the kitchen.

    “Painting one element costs a fraction of painting everything, but still highlights what you want the eye to fall on,” Spanos says. “A gallon of paint and a weekend’s work keeps you under budget.”.

    In addition to going with lower cabinets, you could consider painting an island, pantry door, the trim, or the inside of a glass-front cabinet.

    It has been revealed that to allow your eye to have multiple things to admire in your kitchen, go with a “layered look,” as designers call it. Think: linens, decor, rugs, and artwork.

    Recent findings suggest that spanos says that she has accomplished this look for under $100 in a few projects she’s worked on. In one art-filled home, she carried the creative feel into the kitchen by displaying art on a couple shelves above the sink area. In another kitchen, she laid down a black-and-white geometric rug for visual interest, which tied into the matte black hardware.

    She says, “A few quality tea towels, a small rug or runner, and a piece of art can all be found affordably, especially if you shop vintage or, even better, your own home.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that gift-giving during the holidays is a delicate dance: you want to find the right item that feels thoughtful and cool but also doesn’t kill your budget or feel like something they already own. Our team is passionate about helping people find the right items, from hosting gifts to products you can bring to your next white elephant to even what to put in your family’s stocking stuffers. The topic we’re tackling? Best gifts under $25 that don’t feel tacky or cheap.

    If you dig hard enough, there are actually plenty of unique, thoughtful, and fun finds for under this price point. Whether it be a martini-shaped candle, colorful oven mitts, or a deck of tarot cards, the variety of gift ideas ahead will work for your groups’ gifting needs. These nifty finds are proof that you can buy something that feels special without spending a ton. We’ll raise a glass to that.

    For the person who always orders a martini, gift them this candle that nods to a dirty martini! It has notes of greens, herbs, and juniper to make their home smell fresh. However, they may not even burn it, to keep the wax intact for maximum cuteness on the table.

    The sentimentalist in your life will appreciate a framed photo, especially if they’re moving away, just moved into a new home, or have been talking about filling their space with meaningful items.

    Bedding and towel brand Hommey recently introduced tableware, and the pieces are just as colorful and fun as their sheets. We love these two-toned bowls, perfect for olives, nuts, and other small snacks for gatherings.

    Store-bought lighters aren’t the prettiest, so give them a case to hold their lighter in. This option from Etsy can be personalized, and we’re guessing they’ll want to proudly leave it out on their coffee table right next to their candle.

    Recent findings suggest that everyone talks about their coffee setup, but can we take a moment to talk about a proper matcha setup? Their morning ritual at home isn’t complete without a fun bowl and whisk stand set, and this Anthro pairing comes in many colorful options.

    With winter heading our way, a heated blanket is a must. This soft flannel option comes in a classic plaid pattern that oozes holiday vibes and has 10 adjustable heat settings ranging from 86°F to 122°F.

    If you catch them watching tarot readings on TikTok and YouTube, you know it’s time to get their own deck. This one is perfect for beginners because it comes with thought starters and features cat illustrations for a lighthearted touch.

    Industry observers note that whether they just moved into their first apartment or recently invested in an espresso machine, they will need espresso cups. We love this set because it comes with six earthy shades, so if they have a few guests over, everyone has a cup.

    Not only does a pie bird look adorable in the middle of a piping-hot apple pie, but it makes it taste better too. Pie birds (or whistles) vent steam during the baking process, preventing the filling from boiling over and the crust from getting soggy.

    In a recent development, we had to test this mini water bottle ourselves, and we found it's incredibly handy to take on the go. It's just the right size to fit in a pocket, holding your morning coffee or a drink for the beach.

    It has been revealed that for the friend who loves a vinyl dig or a newly introduced pressing of their favorite artist, help them keep their collection in tip-top shape. This cleaning kit stores easily in a record cabinet, and keeps even the dustiest records sounding brand-new.

    It has been revealed that to fill your newly introduced taper candle holders (and support a small business in the process), snag a set of these hand-poured beeswax taper candles. They add instant drama, and they're paraffin-free. Plus, they're unscented, so they won't clash with the scentscape of your home.

    Sources indicate that art therapy can be a great way to release stress and celebrate your inner child. This takes that joy on the road, with a brush that you only need water to use, and a design that disappears over time. No mess, and no requirement to get every stroke perfect.

    Sources indicate that fluted designs are back in, and this adorable vase is perfect to display a few choice blooms. The U-shaped design also works as standalone decor, if you just want it to be a striking sculpture.

    Though this giant farfalle looks like the real thing, it actually smells more like a traditional candle, with notes of jasmine, neroli, and orange blossom. It also comes in a rigatoni shape, if that's more the recipient's thing.

    In a recent development, of course, you can gift a loved one a candle and a set of matches from the drugstore, but that's hardly any fun. Instead, grab a much more stylish version of the traditional matchbox that they can leave out on display. Worry not; there's a striker on the bottom. The matches, however, are not included!

    Anyone on your list who appreciates the kitschier things in life will adore this ceramic soap dish shaped like a claw-foot bathtub. Just like an actual tub, there is a tiny hole for drainage so that the suds don't sit (and get moldy) in the basin.

    Industry observers note that as far as we're concerned, no one can ever have too many oven mitts. After all, they get stained quickly, so having a fresh, clean pair on hand is always a good idea.

    There's no shame in being afraid of the dark, so we say embrace the fear and snag this charming (and portable) touch lamp. It gets brighter and dimmer with just the tap of a finger. It almost mimics candlelight, but unlike a flickering flame, it is safe to use all night.

    It may be hard to believe that something so artistic is from Amazon, the place we buy our sponges, gym socks, and YETI water bottles, but here we are. You can rest assured that, unlike some of the other goods you may buy on Amazon, this bowl is not made in bulk. In fact, it's from one of the thousands of small businesses that sell their wares on the platform. How's that for a lucky find?

    We’ve had espresso nails, almond milk nails, and now we’re savoring chocolate strawberry nails. So what exactly are they? Think of anything in the family of mocha shades, pinky browns, and deep berry tones. It’s the color you get when a ripe strawberry takes a dip in melted chocolate.

    Industry observers note that the look works because it balances warm and cool. The rich brown base keeps things grounded and neutral, while the berry undertones add a soft flush of color that feels fresh rather than flat. It’s a shade that flatters nearly every skin tone, and it’s subtle enough for the office yet moody enough for a night out. For an extra touch, try a glossy top coat to mimic that just-dipped chocolate shine, or add a thin chrome or sheer pink accent nail for a little dimension.

    Below, we’ve rounded up some fun designs to get you inspired for your next chocolate strawberry manicure.

    Like a strawberry dipped fully in chocolate, this dark shade hides a subtle red glow that peeks through almost like a cat-eye effect.

    This dark berry shade has a high-gloss, mirror-like shine, just like a strawberry fresh from a dip in silky milk chocolate.

    From dreamy cotton-candy pink to a deep, jammy berry, these rosy shades capture every stage of a juicy strawberry, from first blush to fully ripe.

    This nail set looks like creamy milk chocolate glazed under a frosty chrome finish.

    The silver studs on this rich berry shade mimic a strawberry’s tiny seeds, with a glam twist.

    Recent findings suggest that these short nails are neatly filed and glossed to perfection. The rounded shape keeps them practical for everyday wear, while the mirror-bright finish gives them a polished, just-left-the-salon look.

    Industry observers note that this mani pairs a lustrous chocolate base with a sweet pink French tip. The soft pink line adds a playful pop against the deep brown, giving the classic French a fresh, dessert-inspired twist.

    Soft pink polka dots float across a deep burgundy base, a playful nod to retro charm with a ripe, berry-rich finish.

    This manicure features DND’s Strawberry Wine, a moody fall shade that’s hard to beat.

    Another DND color, Fudgsicle, is a rich chocolate brown with a hint of red, the ideal base for chocolate strawberry nails.

    Like real strawberries, the black dots melt into the base so completely they’re nearly invisible, until a closer look reveals the quiet detail hiding in plain sight.

    • Industry observers note that all products featured on Vogue are independently selected by our editors.
    • Some clothes provide utility, some fantasy.
    • Fair Isle knits came to fame under an earlier Prince of Wales (later Edward VIII) in the 1920s, and have remained a favorite of the historically sporty British royal family ever since.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that all products featured on Vogue are independently selected by our editors. However, we may earn affiliate revenue on this article and commission when you buy something.

    Some clothes provide utility, some fantasy. Only a few can conjure an entire mood. A Fair Isle sweater is a mood. It’s the physical embodiment of toasty weekends in farm houses and snowy chalets; the clothing equivalent of hot cocoa and a crackling fireplace—perfectly familiar and never too sweet.

    Fair Isle knits came to fame under an earlier Prince of Wales (later Edward VIII) in the 1920s, and have remained a favorite of the historically sporty British royal family ever since. The late Princess Diana was seen in a perfectly 1980s version in bold neon pink and green, which she paired with neutral corduroy trousers, and later in a classic Christmas-worthy reindeer Fair Isle knit, proving that the heritage hero can’t be put in a box.

    This season, as is par for the course, labels from Dries Van Noten to Marni are giving the fall fashion favorite a fresh spin. Everyday highlights include Polo Ralph Lauren’s turtleneck—as seen in our Cold Weather shop—plus La Ligne’s chunky crewneck, both of which find their match in soft brown corduroy trousers. Toss on a barn jacket and stompy boots and off you go.

    According to recent reports, look to Lisa Yang for a slightly more minimalist take; its pared-back design is perfectly cozy for a weekend gallery stroll, but still sophisticated enough to make an appearance at the office. (We’d layer it underneath an elegant wrap coat or a slouchy leather bomber jacket—both work.) And with ski season quickly approaching, you’re going to want to make a piece from Gigi Hadid’s Guest in Residence collab with Halfdays the centerpiece of all your alpine looks, on and off the piste.

    Between the comfy fits and charming motifs, you won’t mind the cold at all in any of these Fair Isle knits—take a look for yourself.

    #66293. Tech Report: Has Zegna Cracked the Code to Modern Tailoring?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (776 w)

    Tech Report: Has Zegna Cracked the Code to Modern Tailoring?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that pay attention to the world of menswear long enough, and you’ll notice that certain quandaries come up time and again.
    • According to Alessandro Sartori, the artistic director of Zegna for a little more than a decade now, there’s another question we should all be asking ourselves: What exactly is a suit these days?
    • Sources indicate that “Everything we do here is grounded in tailoring techniques and in tailoring fabrics,” Sartori tells me over Zoom from his home in Milan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that pay attention to the world of menswear long enough, and you’ll notice that certain quandaries come up time and again. A favorite among traditionalists and avant-garde types alike is the fate of the suit. It’s been incorrectly declared dead enough times that the handwringing over its demise has largely shifted to questions of its evolving role in the modern guy’s wardrobe: Who wears a suit, and when, and why?

    According to Alessandro Sartori, the artistic director of Zegna for a little more than a decade now, there’s another question we should all be asking ourselves: What exactly is a suit these days?

    Sources indicate that “Everything we do here is grounded in tailoring techniques and in tailoring fabrics,” Sartori tells me over Zoom from his home in Milan. “But I'm a major believer that a suit doesn't necessarily have to be a combination of the classic top and the classic bottom in the same fabric and color.” It can be comprised of those things, he stresses. But the “modern suit,” as he calls it, can also be an intentional pairing of a different kind of top—a chore coat, an overshirt—with a trouser with a different fabrication. The materials and colors should feel complementary and cohesive but needn’t be perfectly matched.

    “This is not only a way to give a newly introduced life to suiting,” he explains, “but to dress men differently—and, at the same time, keep the quality, the craft, and the beautiful fit that a tailored piece has.”.

    The idea is to adapt classic techniques to the realities of getting dressed today. “Many fashion brands offer a nice quality, but is not the handmade quality that we do,” Sartori claims. “And there are a lot of brands that are offering beautiful, beautiful quality, but they are quite classic.” Since he started in 2016, Sartori’s overarching project has been to populate the gulf between those two modes of production, making clothes that feel contemporary but are rooted in the top-tier fabrics and handwork that helped Zegna become the powerhouse of Italian fashion that it is today.

    It has been revealed that the latest addition to Sartori’s lineup is a fresh jacket, the Falcon. It pays homage to the sort of utilitarian jackets Zegna founder Ermenegildo Zegna might have worn while walking the grounds of what is now the Oasi Zegna nature reserve in northern Italy, at the base of the Biellese Alps. (According to company lore, Ermenegildo imagined those walks as being accompanied by the flight of a falcon.).

    Sources indicate that sartori acknowledges that the use case, in 2026, might be a little different. “I don't think that people are necessarily using the jacket walking up in the mountains,” he notes. The Falcon is more about embracing a “sporty-chic attitude,” whether you’re stomping around the country or the city, and working within the modular framework that the designer has created at Zegna. You can mix and match it with other pieces—both old and fresh—from the brand, and you can wear it as part of a “modern suit” or on its own.

    The new design is cut from Zegna’s Oasi Cashmere for lightweight warmth, and Sartori calls it “a great addition to our vocabulary.” Buttoned patch pockets give you somewhere to stash your stuff, a bowling collar can be flipped up to shield against stiff winds, and an internal drawstring can be cinched at the midsection for a little extra protection against the cold. Ultimately, it’s a familiar-looking piece. But it’s exceptional in its construction and materials and its design—a streamlined take on the hunting jackets of yore—is as considered as how it’s made.

    “Long-lasting life is a key factor for what we're doing, and I don't mean only quality-wise,” Sartori says. “I also mean design-wise.”.

    The designer, for his part, hopes that the Falcon—alongside other modern classics from the brand—will be the sort of thing that guys wear and reinterpret for years before passing it on to the next generation. And as the brand continues to grow and evolve alongside its customer base, one of his biggest aims is to ensure that each item he introduces remains relevant throughout its (ideally long) lifespan.

    According to recent reports, “It’s like writing a book, and every season I add a chapter,” he says. “Because the story is going on, is moving with our clients, our community of people, our brand, our family. So many layers are … I don’t want to say ready, but cooking. I see a bright future for the brand, following this principle of walking with our customers and building an indelible aesthetic. I like this approach.”.

    #66291. Before & After: Two Best Friends Turned a Stripped-Down Tudor Into a Colorful, Antique-Filled Dream Home
